title: Evaluate strategies for increasing production

blocks.heading: Evaluate strategies for increasing production
blocks.text: Privatisation is transferring ownership of an enterprise or asset from the state to private owners. A change of ownership may bring investment or altered incentives, but does not itself guarantee higher reliable output, affordable access or environmental protection. Assess a proposal against the stated aim and evidence. New finance can address a broken pump, but service terms, maintenance capability and accountability affect who receives usable water. Retaining state ownership with a feasible repair and management improvement is an alternative. Distinguish an ownership decision from simply hiring a contractor to perform a task.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Weigh two feasible proposals
blocks.text: A fictional water service must increase reliable deliveries. Proposal A transfers ownership and includes financed pump repairs, but its proposed tariff would exclude many low-income users. Proposal B retains state ownership and has funded repairs and maintenance staff but slower procurement. For a goal combining reliability and access, neither ownership label settles the choice. A could suit the aim if access protection is feasible; B could suit it if its delay can be managed. Compare the actual repair, timing and access conditions and explain which is decisive. These are fictional alternatives, not a claim about current Namibian utility policy.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Privatisation: possible benefits and costs
blocks.text: Privatisation transfers a state-owned activity into private ownership. A sale may raise public funds once, but this is not recurring tax revenue. A commercially accountable operator may cut waste, react to customers or invest in new methods. Competition can encourage better quality and restrain prices where customers have genuine alternatives. These gains are conditional: one private monopoly may raise charges instead. Staff reductions can remove jobs; loss of an access obligation can exclude poorer or remote users. Compare investment, efficiency, prices, employment and coverage together. Regulation and the sale terms affect who gains, so changing ownership is not proof of improvement.
